title: Dense-range perfect hash aggregate beyond perfect_ht_threshold
reasons: no visible template faster beyond its noise (best: q13 -3.6%; needs at least -5%)
summary: I changed CanUsePerfectHashAggregate in src/execution/physical_plan/plan_aggregate.cpp. The existing perfect_ht_threshold check works as before. Above that threshold, a GROUP BY can still use the perfect hash aggregate if three guards hold: (1) the total key bits are at most max(threshold, 22); (2) the key range is dense, meaning op.estimated_cardinality is at least 2^bits/4; (3) the tables fit in memory: threads * 2^bits * (sum of aligned aggregate state sizes + 1) must be at most 1/8 of the buffer manager's max memory, because these tables are allocated outside the buffer manager and cannot spill. The distinct and combine checks still apply to both paths. A user who sets the threshold above 22 sees the same behaviour as before. The setting's default is unchanged. On q13 the inner aggregate is now a PERFECT_HASH_GROUP_BY and its operator time fell from 3.14s to 0.53s. In the profile, total time went from 1.09s to 0.92s. `bench` (a quick check: 2 bindings, 4 hot runs each) measured q13 at 781.4ms before and 716.8ms after, 8.3% faster; it reported matching results. The build passes.
notes: The group key in q13 is the compressed uinteger form of the key (range about 1.5M, so 21 bits with the +2). The estimated cardinality was about 1.15M groups against 2.1M slots, about 55% full, so it passes the density guard comfortably. The memory guard only counts fixed state sizes; any extra memory an aggregate allocates in its arena (strings, lists) is not counted, which is also true of the existing perfect hash path. Each thread allocates and initialises 2^bits slots, and Combine/finalize scan every slot. If more threads ever make that overhead show up, a follow-up could make the 1/4 density factor or the 22-bit cap scale with the thread count. In q13 the next big costs are the HASH_JOIN (1.9s) and the LIKE filter in the orders scan (2.7s).

title: Skip redundant found-match stores in RIGHT/FULL join probe
reasons: abandoned by the implementer after investigation
summary: I changed two spots in src/execution/join_hashtable.cpp so the found-match flag is only written when it is still false. The first is the PropagatesBuildSide marking loop in ScanStructure. The second is the non-equality branch of NextRightSemiOrAntiJoin. The build succeeded (BUILD OK) and results matched in every bench run. Five bench runs of q13 against the current best gave -11.5%, +9.5%, -11.7%, +16.4% and +4.0%, which averages about +1.6% (slower). The swings are much bigger than any effect. One profile of q13.m0 showed the HASH_JOIN operator at 1.92s, against 2.15s in .dbe/profile.md. That is only one sample, and operator times are as noisy as the wall times. I see no reliable wall-time gain, so the change is unlikely to clear the 5% bar.
notes: Wall time on q13 is very noisy, with ±15% swings between bench runs. That noise hides any gain from cache-coherence savings on the found flags. These stores may not be the bottleneck anyway. On q13 the bigger costs are HASH_GROUP_BY at 2.93s and the orders TABLE_SCAN with its LIKE filter at 2.75s, while HASH_JOIN is about 1.9-2.1s. If you retry this idea, combine it with something else or run many more timing repetitions. The likelier wins are the grouped aggregate on the join key (1.5M groups, count) or the NOT LIKE filter scan.

title: Parallel combine and parallel source for large perfect hash aggregate (re-land E0001)
summary:
I re-landed E0001 and made the large perfect hash aggregate parallel in both its combine and its source. q13 went from 706.8 ms to 575.5 ms (-18.6%) on the quick bench (2 bindings, 4 hot runs each). The tree builds in release (BUILD OK).

Changes:
(a) plan_aggregate.cpp: CanUsePerfectHashAggregate now accepts up to max(perfect_ht_threshold, 22) total bits. Beyond the threshold, two guards must also pass. Density: estimated_cardinality >= 2^bits/4, and an estimate must exist. Memory: threads * 2^bits * (sum of aligned state sizes + 1) <= max_memory/8. The path at or below the threshold is unchanged.
(b) PerfectAggregateHashTable has new methods. CombineRange(other, begin, end, ArenaAllocator&) combines only slots [begin, end) using the caller's arena. StoreAllocator(other) and StoreAllocator(unique_ptr<ArenaAllocator>) take ownership of arenas. A Scan overload takes an end position, a caller-owned address vector and an arena, so concurrent scans of disjoint ranges are safe. Combine and the old Scan now call these, with the same behaviour as before.
(c) PhysicalPerfectHashAggregate::Combine: tables with at least 2^16 slots are split into at most 64 stripes, each a multiple of STANDARD_VECTOR_SIZE and together covering every slot, each with its own mutex. Each thread starts at stripe (atomic++ % count), visits every stripe in rotation with its own arena, then under the global lock stores that arena and the local table's arena. Smaller tables keep the exact old single-lock Combine.
(d) Parallel source: ParallelSource() returns true and there is a new local source state with its own address vector and arena. Large tables hand out blocks of 16384 slots through an atomic counter, and MaxThreads is the number of blocks. Small tables use one block covering the whole table, so MaxThreads is 1 and the scan stays serial as before.

Correctness check: I grouped on an integer key, which plans as PERFECT_HASH_GROUP_BY (confirmed with EXPLAIN), using min on a string column, sum, count(*) and len(list(...)). I compared the result with the same query grouped on the key cast to varchar, which uses the radix hash aggregate. The hash sums were identical.
notes:
The main lesson: E0001 alone gave only 3.6%, because the serial combine and the serial scan over 2M slots also made the outer aggregate pipeline single-threaded. Parallelising the source mattered as much as the faster sink.

Choices I made:
- Each scan thread finalizes states with its own arena, and that arena is kept until the local source state is destroyed. I don't reset it per chunk, which matches the old lifetime of the shared arena.
- Each state is still destroyed exactly once per table: the global table destroys its own slots, and each local table destroys its own.
- Each thread's local table is still filled with initial states for all 2^bits slots. That initialization runs once per thread and is accepted by the memory guard.

Possible follow-ups:
- Skip scan blocks that have no set slots by using a coarse occupancy bitmap.
- Let the local sink tables start out lazily or sparsely to cut that per-thread initialization cost.

title: Perfect hash join for RIGHT joins on dense unique build keys
summary:
I extended the perfect hash join to RIGHT outer joins (build side preserved) and allowed dense build key ranges up to 2^22. Measured on q13: the bench went from 563.4 to 448.8 ms (-20.3%). The HASH_JOIN operator dropped from 1.87s to 0.19s CPU. The only new cost is 0.16s in the decompress projection above the join, because it now gets dictionary vectors.

Changes:
1) perfect_hash_join_executor.cpp, CanDoPerfectHashJoin:
   - Accepts JoinType::RIGHT as well as INNER, with the same single integer-equality condition.
   - Bails out if the build min or max is NULL.
   - Allows build ranges between 2^20 and 2^22 only if two guards hold. Density: Count*4 >= range+1. Memory: slots*(8+1+sum of rhs_output type sizes) <= max_memory/8.
   - Fixed an off-by-one in the duplicate early-out: it was `Count > range` and is now `Count > range+1`. The old check rejected every fully dense unique key set, for INNER joins too. It is only a heuristic; the build fill still detects duplicates exactly.
2) The build fill now skips NULL keys. RIGHT-join hash tables keep rows with NULL keys but leave has_null false, so without this the garbage key value of a NULL row could match.
3) For joins that propagate the build side:
   - FullScanHashTable records slot_to_row (the tuple address of each slot) and a zeroed per-slot slot_found byte array.
   - ProbePerfectHashTable sets slot_found for every matched slot.
   - A new PerfectHashJoinExecutor::PropagateFoundMatches() stores true at row+tuple_size for each found slot. This is the same flag JoinHashTable::ScanFullOuter reads. It is called from HashJoinGlobalSourceState::PrepareScanHT under the source lock, after the probe pipeline has finished, so the existing full-outer scan works unchanged. The tuple pointers stay valid because ScanKeyColumn pins with KEEP_EVERYTHING_PINNED.
4) join_filter_pushdown_optimizer.cpp: `compute_aggregates_anyway` now also covers RIGHT joins, so the build min/max is computed even when no table scan takes the pushed filter. Without this the RIGHT join never got a range: here the probe keys sit behind a compress projection.

Correctness checks all matched the same query forced onto the regular join (keys cast to VARCHAR). They covered:
- NULL build keys with a 2M range on the large path
- NULL probe keys
- unmatched build rows
- VARCHAR and DOUBLE build output columns
- a sparse range (keys spaced by 3)
- duplicate build keys, which fall back to the regular join
- an empty probe side, which outputs all build rows
- a single-row build
- an all-NULL build
- INNER joins on dense keys
- customer/orders LEFT and RIGHT joins with selective ON predicates
notes:
My first build showed no effect (-4%, which is noise) because two more gates outside the issue's plan blocked the path:
(a) JoinFilterPushdownOptimizer computes min/max aggregates without a probe-side scan target only for INNER joins.
(b) The duplicate early-out `Count > build_range` was off by one, so a fully dense key set 1..N was always rejected. This also affected INNER joins before this change.

Things to know:
- RIGHT-join hash tables store rows with NULL keys but do not set has_null, so any perfect-path code must check key validity.
- Concurrent writes of the found byte are plain stores of the same value.

Follow-ups:
- The decompress projection above the join now gets dictionary vectors (0.16s CPU). A compress/decompress pair around the join that cancels out could be removed.
- The PERFECT_HASH_GROUP_BY (0.45s) and the scan (2.47s, a string LIKE filter) now dominate q13.

title: SWAR first+last-byte candidate scan in FindStrInStr for short haystacks
reasons: no visible template faster beyond its noise (best: q13 -4.8%; needs at least -5%)
summary:
I added a block-wise substring search to FindStrInStr in src/function/scalar/string/contains.cpp, using the first and last needle byte to filter candidates (Muła-style strstr). It applies when the needle is at least 2 bytes and the haystack is at most 256 bytes, on little-endian GCC/Clang builds.

How it works:
- With SSE2, it checks 16 candidate positions per step. It compares haystack+i against needle[0] and haystack+i+n-1 against needle[n-1], ANDs the two results, and takes a movemask.
- Otherwise it uses an 8-byte SWAR version with an exact zero-byte mask, so the mask has no false positives.
- Only the candidates that survive get a memcmp of the middle n-2 bytes. Set bits are visited from low to high, so the leftmost match is still returned.
- Positions left over at the end are covered by one overlapping final block, shifted to drop positions already checked, instead of a scalar loop. Every load stays inside [haystack, haystack+size), so there is no over-read.
- Haystacks shorter than n-1+8 use a small scalar loop. Long haystacks, 1-byte needles and other builds keep the original memchr path.

Measured with bench, my build against the current best:
- First version with a scalar tail loop: q13 only -2% to -3%.
- With the overlapping final block: q13 456.0 → 401.6 ms (-11.9%), then 458.3 → 404.1 ms (-11.8%) on a second run. Visible geomean -11.8%.

Correctness checks, comparing against a brute-force reference written in SQL (substr equality plus list_position):
- 200k random strings on alphabet {a,b,c}, haystacks 0-60 bytes, needles 1-6 bytes: 0 mismatches.
- 50k strings with haystacks 0-300 bytes and needles 2-20 bytes on a skewed alphabet, which gives many partial and overlapping matches: 0 mismatches, and LIKE '%n%' agreed with strpos.
- 100k strings of multibyte UTF-8 characters, also checking ILIKE: 0 mismatches.
- Hand-picked cases also gave the right answers: repeated prefixes, matches at the start and end, needle longer than the haystack, two-segment LIKE in either order, a 300+ byte haystack that takes the memchr path, and string_split with a multi-character delimiter.
notes:
The overlapping final block is what made this pay off. A first version with a scalar tail loop (up to 7 branchy positions per string) gave only -2% to -3%, because on ~50-byte strings the remainder handling cost about as much as the memchr calls it replaced.

Single-thread timings of the sql tool on this machine are very noisy (±30%), so use bench for decisions.

A NOT contains / NOT LIKE scan is still about 2x slower than length(col)>45 at 1 thread. Part of that is probably FSST decode and dereferencing non-inlined strings, which a comparison like `<> 'zz'` mostly avoids by checking the inline prefix. Follow-up ideas:
- An AVX2 path under target attributes.
- A first/last-byte filter that runs directly on FSST-decoded buffers.
- Fusing LIKE segment searches so the second segment starts from the first segment's match without per-call overhead.

title: Reuse a per-scan-state string heap for FSST decoded strings
reasons: abandoned by the implementer after investigation
summary: I built the planned change, but it made no measurable difference to q13, so I'm abandoning it. What it does: `ColumnScanState` holds one cached `buffer_ptr<VectorBuffer> cached_string_buffer`. A new helper, `GetDecompressStringBuffer`, in fsst.cpp is used by `StringScanPartial` (the non-FSST-vector branch) and by `FSSTStorage::Select`. It applies when result_offset is 0, the result has no auxiliary and the vector is FLAT. In that case it reuses the cached buffer if use_count()==1, after calling a new `VectorStringBuffer::ResetForReuse()` (resets the arena, which keeps its largest block, and clears the references). Otherwise it creates a new buffer with the result's allocator, the same way `GetStringBuffer` does, and installs it with `SetAuxiliary`. The build succeeded and results matched (bench's correctness check passed). q13 bench against the current best: 489.9 vs 473.7 ms (-3.3%) on the first run and 457.8 vs 458.6 ms (+0.2%) on the second, which is noise. The orders TABLE_SCAN in the profile stayed at about 2.4–3.1s, also within noise. I did not add instrumentation, so I never confirmed that the reuse path actually triggers in this plan. It is still clear that allocation is not where the decode time goes.
notes: The hypothesis was wrong. About 7 arena mallocs per 2048-row vector is tiny next to roughly 100ns per string of FSST decode plus the pushed-down NOT LIKE filter. After warm-up, glibc's dynamic mmap threshold probably serves those blocks from the heap rather than fresh pages, so there is little page-fault cost to remove. The optional pre-reserve step (3) would not help either, for the same reason. The o_comment cost is the decode itself and the LIKE evaluation over decoded strings. Better directions are a faster decode path, such as decompressing straight into a contiguous per-vector buffer without the len*8 shrinkable alloc and finalize per string, or running the LIKE match on decoded bytes without materialising string_t. Note that the diff changes two widely included headers (vector_buffer.hpp, scan_state.hpp), which costs a 10+ minute rebuild.
